title: Much ado about PuFins
gist: Resolution Foundation argues the UK's public financial institutions -- the 'PuFins' -- are the mechanism by which Andy Burnham can keep the existing fiscal rules while raising investment, because the October 2024 switch of the debt target to Public Sector Net Financial Liabilities gives the financial assets they acquire more favourable accounting treatment than conventional capital spending. It recommends channelling GBP 16 billion of extra capital into the National Wealth Fund over five years to match the European Investment Bank's pre-referendum scale, at a direct cost of around GBP 400 million a year in debt interest, and warns against letting PuFins issue their own bonds, which would cost roughly 10 per cent more than gilt funding with no accounting benefit.

themes.theme: Fiscal rule arbitrage via financial assets

insights.claim: The October 2024 rewrite of the UK's fiscal rules, which shifted the debt target to Public Sector Net Financial Liabilities, gives financial assets acquired by public financial institutions more favourable accounting treatment than conventional capital spending, making them a particularly important channel for raising investment.
insights.speaker: Elliott Christensen
insights.so_what: The definitional change creates a structural incentive to route UK public investment through loans, equity and guarantees rather than direct capex -- expect deal flow to follow the accounting treatment.
insights.locator: But the rewrite of the fiscal rules in October 2024

insights.claim: Public financial institutions are presented as the route by which a Prime Minister committed to the existing fiscal rules can still deliver a higher-investment economy, resolving what looks like a binding constraint.
insights.speaker: Elliott Christensen
insights.so_what: If adopted, UK investment expansion arrives as balance-sheet activity rather than departmental spending -- a signal to watch state-backed co-investment rather than Budget capex lines.
insights.locator: This briefing note examines the UK’s public financial institutions

insights.claim: The Starmer Government has already almost doubled the balance sheet capacity of the UK's largest public financial institutions, so the expansion of this channel predates the new premiership.
insights.speaker: Elliott Christensen
insights.so_what: Establishes the trend is already in motion -- further increases are incremental policy continuation rather than a regime break, which raises the probability of delivery.
insights.locator: The Starmer Government has already almost doubled

themes.theme: Specific recommendation: scale the National Wealth Fund

insights.claim: Matching the European Investment Bank's pre-referendum scale of operations in the UK would mean boosting National Wealth Fund investments by GBP 16 billion over the next five years.
insights.speaker: Elliott Christensen
insights.so_what: A concrete GBP 16 billion five-year pipeline benchmark -- the number to test any government announcement against, and a sizing input for co-investors in UK infrastructure and industrial projects.
insights.locator: Matching the European Investment Bank’s pre-referendum scale

insights.claim: The GBP 16 billion National Wealth Fund expansion would carry a direct cost of only around GBP 400 million a year in debt interest, before accounting for the returns the acquired financial assets would generate.
insights.speaker: Elliott Christensen
insights.so_what: A 2.5 percent implied carry cost against potential asset returns makes this an unusually cheap way to raise headline investment -- low fiscal resistance means high adoption odds.
insights.locator: This would come at a direct cost of around £400 million a year

insights.claim: The National Wealth Fund is recommended as the first-instance recipient of extra capital among the UK's public financial institutions, rather than spreading funds across the set.
insights.speaker: Elliott Christensen
insights.so_what: Concentration guidance means NWF mandate and sector priorities become the practical determinant of where UK state co-investment lands.
insights.locator: The new Burnham Government should seize this opportunity

insights.claim: Asking public financial institutions to issue their own bonds would cost around 10 per cent more than funding them through gilts, with no more favourable accounting treatment in return -- so it should be resisted.
insights.speaker: Elliott Christensen
insights.so_what: Kills the case for a separate agency bond market in the UK -- relevant to fixed income desks anticipating new sterling SSA supply.
insights.quote: One thing the Prime Minister should resist is asking PuFins to issue their own bonds, which would cost around 10 per cent more than funding them through gilts, with no more favourable accounting treatment in return.
insights.locator: One thing the Prime Minister should resist

themes.theme: Structural drivers of the PuFin build-out

insights.claim: Three forces have pushed public financial institutions toward the centre of UK economic policy: the UK's departure from the European Investment Bank, a renewed focus on industrial policy, and greater recognition of chronic underinvestment.
insights.speaker: Elliott Christensen
insights.so_what: All three drivers are structural and persistent, implying the state co-investment channel keeps growing across political cycles rather than reversing.
insights.locator: These bodies have moved towards the centre of economic policy

insights.claim: Over little more than a decade successive UK governments have built and rebuilt a set of institutions that use public money to provide loans, equity investments and guarantees to the private sector.
insights.speaker: Elliott Christensen
insights.so_what: Repeated institutional churn is itself a risk: private co-investors face mandate and continuity uncertainty when underwriting long-dated UK projects.
